newsitem.title: FRANCE: ALPINE SKIING-WIBERG AND SYKORA STAY ON THE WINNING TRACK.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-WIBERG AND SYKORA STAY ON THE WINNING TRACK.

text.p: Pernilla Wiberg used a chaotic weekend in Austria to move closer to her first overall World Cup title while Thomas Sykora outclassed the opposition once again with a brilliant slalom win in the French Alps.

Wiberg kept her composure when miserable weather forced the organisers in Bad Kleinkirchheim to call off Friday's downhill, then finished an excellent fifth in a downhill won by Swiss Heidi Zurbriggen the next day before going on to win a Super-G on Sunday.
The 26-year-old Swedish all-rounder's fourth World Cup victory this season allowed her to increase her leading total in the overall standings to 863 points.
She is now 214 points ahead of titleholder Katja Seizinger of Germany, third in Sunday's race behind second-placed Isolde Kostner of Italy.
"The weather was perfect today," said a delighted Wiberg. "The slope was hardened by the cold overnight temperatures. It was icy and that's just the way I like it."

While his rivals struggled on a piste hardened by cold temperatures, Sykora mastered the conditions in the ski village of Chamonix to take victory by a massive 1.66 seconds over compatriot Thomas Stangassinger.
"I'm not getting tired of winning," he said. "Every time is different. I've got no explanation for the form I'm in. It's just great."
Sykora, who has won four of the five slaloms held so far this winter while finishing second in the other, dominates the slalom the way Alberto Tomba once did.

The flamboyant Italian, who has had a troubled start to the season, went to bed with flu after clocking the second fastest time in the first leg. His manager later said he would miss a giant slalom on Tuesday in Adelboden and hoped to be back for a slalom on Sunday in Wengen.

Tomba's illness was bad news for the many Italian fans who had crossed the border to cheer their hero on. But they were not too sad as Kristian Ghedina had given them something to celebrate by winning a downhill on Saturday.

His sixth World Cup downhill victory has made Ghedina the most successful downhiller in Italian ski history with one more win than compatriot Herbert Plank, who won five downhills between 1974 and 1980 while battling with the great Austrian Franz Klammer.

The cheerful 27-year-old Ghedina, whose career nearly ended in a terrible car crash in 1991, was just one hundredth of a second ahead of second-placed Atle Skaardal of Norway and 0.11 seconds ahead of Austrian Werner Franz who came third.
The victory allowed Ghedina to catch leader Luc Alphand, who had to be content with fifth place, in the World Cup downhill standings. Both have 365 points.

Giant slalom specialist Michael von Gruenigen of Switzerland came fourth in Sunday's slalom to take first place in the overall World Cup standings from Austrian Hans Knauss, who skied out in the second leg.

"I'm delighted because one of my goals this season was to do well in slaloms," said Von Gruenigen. "I'm not bothered about the World Cup as I can't possibly win it because I only enter two events (the giant slalom and the slalom). I don't want to think about it. What I'm looking forward to is the race in Adelboden. To win there before my fans would be fantastic."
Knauss, who does not usually race slaloms, took part because he hoped to score points in the weekend's first combined event of the season, based on Sunday's race and Saturday's downhill.
Austrian Guenther Mader won the combined event ahead of Norway's Kjetil-Andre Aamodt and Swiss Bruno Kernen.

Wiberg, whose goal this winter is to win the World Cup titles in downhill and slalom, travels next weekend to Zwiesel, Germany, where three women's races, two giant slaloms and a slalom, are scheduled.
Sykora and Ghedina will meanwhile be in Wengen, Switzerland, where a downhill and a slalom are on the men's agenda.
